screens.title: Physics Materials & Rigidbody Constraints
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how Unity lets you shape physical interactions with two complementary tools: Physics Materials and Rigidbody Constraints. Physics Materials let you define how surfaces interact by setting friction and bounciness. Rigidbody Constraints let you freeze motion or rotation on specific axes so objects behave predictably in your game. Together these tools move you beyond basic Colliders and Rigidbodies into precise, play-tested behaviors. We’ll show concrete examples: making an ice surface that causes sliding, creating a super-bouncy rubber ball, and constraining a character so it doesn’t tip over. You’ll also learn common pitfalls, such as fighting the physics system by resetting transforms instead of using constraints, and how combine modes change collision outcomes. By the end you should be able to choose friction and bounce values for terrain, assign materials to colliders, and apply constraints to prevent unwanted motion. Think about a level where the player slides on ice while moving heavy crates — you’ll see how small settings produce distinct, predictable gameplay. Ready to build more controlled interactions? Let’s explore the topics and practical steps.

screens.title: What is a Physics Material?
screens.narratorSegment: A Physics Material is an asset that defines how two surfaces interact when they collide. It packages three essential concepts: static friction, dynamic friction, and bounciness. Static friction resists the onset of motion, so a high static friction means an object sitting on a slope or surface needs more force to start moving. Dynamic friction applies once the object is already sliding, controlling how quickly it slows down. Bounciness, or restitution, controls how much collision energy is retained — zero means no bounce, one is a perfectly elastic collision. These properties are not applied in isolation; Unity also uses combine modes to resolve interactions between two materials. For example, a rubber ball hitting slippery ice will use a combination rule to determine the effective friction and bounce. A common misconception is thinking friction values correspond to real-world units; instead treat them as tuning parameters that shape feel in play mode. As a concrete example, creating a 'SuperBouncy' material with low friction and high bounce will make a sphere both slide and rebound, while a 'SlipperyIce' material with very low static and dynamic friction and low bounce will allow extended sliding with little rebound. The key takeaway is to think of Physics Materials as design tools for predictable interaction rather than exact physical replicas.

content.html:
Core Concept What is a Physics Material?
Definition

An asset that sets how two colliders interact by defining friction and bounciness and how those values combine at runtime.

Static Friction
Resistance when an object is at rest. Higher value makes it harder to start moving.
Dynamic Friction
Resistance while sliding. Controls how quickly motion decays.
Bounciness
Energy retained after collision; 0 means no bounce, 1 is perfectly elastic.
Concrete Example
Imagine a rubber ball with high bounciness and a wood floor with moderate friction. The ball will rebound strongly but slow more quickly if the floor's dynamic friction is higher. If you give the floor a very low friction value, the ball will also slide more after contact. You control these results by setting the material values and testing in play mode.
Common Mistake
Assuming numbers represent real units. Treat values as tuning knobs for gameplay feel.
Key Takeaway
Use Physics Materials to design the game’s tactile feel and iterate in small scenes for predictable outcomes.

screens.title: Creating and Assigning a Physics Material
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a Physics Material in Unity is a simple workflow that yields immediate, testable results. Start in the Project window, right-click, choose Create → Physics Material, and give it a descriptive name like 'SlipperyIce' or 'SuperBouncy.' Open the material and set Dynamic Friction, Static Friction, and Bounciness to your desired values. Next choose Friction Combine and Bounce Combine modes that reflect how you want interactions to resolve when two materials meet. After configuration, select the GameObject with a Collider and drag the new Physics Material into the Collider's Material field in the Inspector. Run the scene and observe collisions to refine values. A useful habit is to create small test scenes with a plane and a sphere to iterate quickly. If you need the surface to always be slippery regardless of the other object, consider using Minimum for friction to favor the lower value. Remember to test both static and dynamic behavior: place an object on the surface to observe static friction, and nudge it or drop it to observe dynamic friction and bounciness. This process-focused approach keeps tuning efficient and repeatable.

SuperBouncy

screens.title: Static vs Dynamic Friction
screens.narratorSegment: Static and dynamic friction address two distinct phases of motion and both matter for believable interactions. Static friction is what keeps a resting object from sliding: it resists the initial force you apply. Dynamic friction comes into play after the object is moving; it slows the object while it slides or rolls. Consider a crate on a slope: if static friction is high, the crate will not start sliding until you apply a significant push. Once it starts sliding, the dynamic friction controls how quickly it slows down. This distinction matters for gameplay because you may want objects that resist small nudges but still slide freely once pushed, or surfaces that are equally reluctant to start and continue sliding. A common misconception is setting static lower than dynamic; typically static should be equal or higher than dynamic to simulate realistic stick-slip behavior. In practice, tune static for how hard it is to start movement, and dynamic for how objects behave while moving. Use concrete tests: place an object at rest to observe static friction, apply force to observe the threshold, then observe sliding to refine dynamic friction. This approach gives you control over both initiation and sustained motion.

keyIdea.title: Two-phase friction control
keyIdea.text: Static friction resists starting movement; dynamic friction resists continued motion. Tune both to shape how objects begin and continue to slide.

content.html:
Comparison Static vs Dynamic
Static Friction

Applied when an object is at rest. Higher values mean more force required to begin moving.

Concrete Example
A heavy crate on a rough floor can sit without moving until pushed hard enough; static friction sets that threshold.
Dynamic Friction

Applied while an object is sliding. Controls how quickly it decelerates once in motion.

Common Mistake
Setting dynamic higher than static can produce unnatural stick-slip. Generally static ≥ dynamic yields predictable results.
Test Workflow
  • Place object at rest to validate static friction.
  • Apply a small force to find the threshold to move.
  • Observe sliding to tune dynamic friction for desired deceleration.

screens.title: Bounciness and Combine Modes
screens.narratorSegment: Bounciness determines how much kinetic energy a collision keeps. Zero bounciness looks like clay: the object won't rebound. High bounciness resembles rubber or a super ball. Unity resolves a collision between two materials by applying the chosen Bounce Combine mode. Modes typically include Average, Minimum, Maximum, and Multiply. Average takes the mean of two bounciness values, Minimum picks the lower, Maximum picks the higher, and Multiply scales them together. The same concept applies to friction with Friction Combine modes. For example, if a rubber ball hits a sticky surface, using Maximum for bounce lets the higher bounciness dominate so the ball still appears lively. Using Minimum for friction means a slippery surface will remain slippery even against a high-friction object. A practical tip: Multiply often produces realistic friction because it scales down when either surface is low in friction; try it when you want surfaces to preserve 'weakness' like ice. A misconception is assuming bounce is independent of mass; while bounciness influences rebound, mass and collision context still affect final motion. Test bounciness with controlled drops and tune combine modes to achieve the intended gameplay effect.

keyIdea.text: Use bounce to control rebound energy and combine modes to decide which material properties win when surfaces interact.

content.html:
Core Concept Bounciness & Combine Modes
Bounciness Explained

Controls energy preserved after a collision. Values near zero absorb energy; values near one preserve energy and create high rebounds.

High Bounce
Rubber-like rebound, use for lively balls.
Low Bounce
Clay or heavy objects that do not rebound.
Combine Modes
Average · Minimum · Maximum · Multiply
Example
Rubber (0.8) + Ice (0.1): Multiply → 0.08 (low), Maximum → 0.8 (high), Minimum → 0.1, Average → 0.45
Testing Tip
Drop or throw objects in a small scene to observe bounce height variations with different combine modes and adjust to match gameplay expectations.

screens.title: Friction Combine Modes: Practical Choices
screens.narratorSegment: Friction Combine modes determine the effective friction when two Physics Materials meet. Average calculates the mean of both friction values, which often produces moderate results. Minimum picks the lower of the two values, and is useful when you want a slippery surface to remain slippery despite contact with a rough object — for example, ice that stays slick even when a heavy boot collides with it. Maximum picks the higher value, which you might use when you want at least one object to contribute high friction, such as a highly grippy boot contacting any floor. Multiply multiplies the two values together and often produces realistic outcomes by scaling friction down when either surface is low. Consider numeric examples: 0.2 * 0.8 = 0.16 shows how Multiply yields lower combined friction when one surface is slippery. A common design choice is Multiply for friction and Maximum or Average for bounce depending on how you want bounciness to show. The practical workflow is to try each combine mode in a small test and choose the mode that matches your physical intuition and gameplay needs.

content.html:
Process Friction Combine Modes
Average
Mean of both values. Good for balanced results.
Minimum
Takes the lower value. Keeps slippery surfaces slippery.
Maximum
Takes the higher value. Ensures at least one surface grips strongly.
Multiply
Multiplies values. Often realistic for friction scaling.
Numeric Example
Material A: 0.8, Material B: 0.2 → Average 0.5, Minimum 0.2, Maximum 0.8, Multiply 0.16. Multiply reduces combined friction when either is low.

screens.title: Applying Materials to Colliders
screens.narratorSegment: Physics Materials are applied to Collider components. Common colliders include Mesh Collider, Box Collider, Sphere Collider, and Plane. When you drag a Physics Material onto a Collider's Material field in the Inspector, that Collider inherits friction and bounciness settings for collisions. Remember that the collision outcome uses both colliders' materials and their combine modes, so both sides matter. In a scene where a ball rolls on a floor, you typically assign a material to both the ball's Sphere Collider and the ground's Mesh or Plane Collider to achieve the intended interaction. A useful architecture approach is to keep commonly used materials in a 'Materials' project folder with descriptive names like SuperBouncy and SlipperyIce, then reuse them across objects. If many objects share the same behavior, reusing a single Physics Material reduces maintenance and avoids inconsistent results. When debugging unexpected behavior, check collider assignments first, then Rigidbody mass and constraints; often surprising collisions come from an unassigned or incorrectly combined material rather than code errors. Applying Materials to Colliders means attach physics materials to each collider that participates in collisions and manage them centrally for consistent behavior.. In practical terms, where and how to attach materials for desired interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition Assign to Colliders
Where to attach

  • Mesh or Plane Collider — for terrain and floors.

2. Are combine modes appropriate for design?

content.html:
Example PushBall Script
Starter Code
using UnityEngine;

public class PushBall : MonoBehaviour
{
  public float pushForce = 200f;

  void Start()
  {
    Rigidbody rb = GetComponent();
    if (rb != null)
    {
      // Apply a force to push the ball forward and slightly up
      rb.AddForce(transform.forward * pushForce + Vector3.up * (pushForce / 5), ForceMode.Impulse);
    }
  }
}
Tip
Change pushForce in the inspector to compare how different initial energies interact with materials.
Mistake to Avoid
Do not set transform.position or transform.rotation every frame to stop motion; use constraints instead.

screens.title: Rigidbody Constraints Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Rigidbody Constraints live on the Rigidbody component and let you freeze position and rotation on the X, Y, and Z axes. Use them to prevent unwanted motion like vertical drifting or tipping while still allowing other degrees of freedom. For instance, freezing Rotation X and Rotation Z keeps a character upright while leaving Rotation Y free for turning. Freezing Position Y prevents up-and-down movement when an object should slide on a plane. screens.title: Rolling Ball Puzzle: Materials and Constraints
screens.narratorSegment: Consider a rolling ball puzzle where the ball must roll freely across the floor but should not fly off the plane or tip into impossible orientations. Start with a Sphere Collider and Rigidbody. For material choices, give the ball a Physics Material like 'RubberBall' with high bounciness and moderate friction if you want lively rebounds. Give the ground 'WoodFloor' or 'SlipperyIce' depending on desired slide. If the game enforces a strict flat play area, you can freeze Position Y to prevent vertical movement if the design is strictly 2D-like. More commonly, allow gravity and collisions to handle vertical movement, and rely on constraints only for rotations you want to prevent — for example, freeze Rotation X and Rotation Z if you want the ball to remain upright for a character-like ball. For true rolling behavior, keep rotations enabled and avoid freezing rotation axes. Test several runs: change materials, run the scene, and observe bounce and slide. If collisions feel jittery after adding many constraints, back off constraints and consider adjusting mass or collision geometry. This scenario highlights trade-offs between physical freedom and gameplay control.

Scenario Rolling Ball Puzzle
Design Steps

screens.title: Safety Notes & Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: When working with Physics Materials and Rigidbody Constraints there are recurring pitfalls to avoid. First, do not fight the physics solver by constantly resetting transform. position or transform. rotation in Update; this causes jitter and unstable collisions. Use Rigidbody Constraints instead to freeze axes. Second, avoid over-constraint: freezing too many axes can make the solver struggle under large forces and occasionally let objects pass through each other or behave strangely. Third, keep collision geometry simple and use compound colliders when needed: complex Mesh Colliders interacting at high speed increase instability. Fourth, be mindful of performance when you have many distinct Physics Materials and complex colliders — excessively complex setups can increase overhead. Test each change in isolated scenes with repeatable impulses or drops so you can clearly see the effect of a single change. Finally, when results seem wrong, check the Rigidbody mass, interpolation settings, collision detection mode, and whether colliders overlap at start. Addressing these items early avoids confusing behavior and saves iteration time during playtesting. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how Unity lets you shape physical interactions with two complementary tools: Physics Materials and Rigidbody Constraints. Physics Materials let you define how surfaces interact by setting friction and bounciness. Rigidbody Constraints let you freeze motion or rotation on specific axes so objects behave predictably in your game. Together these tools move you beyond basic Colliders and Rigidbodies into precise, play-tested behaviors. We’ll show concrete examples: making an ice surface that causes sliding, creating a super-bouncy rubber ball, and constraining a character so it doesn’t tip over. You’ll also learn common pitfalls, such as fighting the physics system by resetting transforms instead of using constraints, and how combine modes change collision outcomes. By the end you should be able to choose friction and bounce values for terrain, assign materials to colliders, and apply constraints to prevent unwanted motion. Think about a level where the player slides on ice while moving heavy crates — you’ll see how small settings produce distinct, predictable gameplay. Ready to build more controlled interactions? Let’s explore the topics and practical steps.

Over the next set of slides you will develop four measurable skills. First, you will understand the purpose and application of Physics Materials in Unity — knowing what friction and bounciness represent and when to use them. Second, you will learn to configure dynamic and static friction and bounciness values, and how combine modes change outcomes when two surfaces meet. Third, you will practice applying Physics Materials to Colliders so surface behavior takes effect in the scene. Fourth, you will use Rigidbody Constraints to freeze motion or rotation on specific axes. Each skill focuses on predictable physics: testing values in play mode, choosing combine modes for consistent results, and avoiding common mistakes like manipulating transforms every frame. These skills matter because small changes in friction or constraints change gameplay feel dramatically — slippery ice, sticky tar, or a stable character are achieved by intentional choices. Expect hands-on practice creating materials, assigning them, and testing a bouncy ball scenario that demonstrates how materials and constraints interact.

This second objectives slide expands how you’ll practice each skill with concrete scenarios. You will create materials like Ice and SuperBouncy, assign them to ground and spheres, and observe sliding and bounce in play mode. You will try different Friction Combine and Bounce Combine modes to see how Average, Minimum, Maximum, and Multiply change outcomes when two materials meet. You will apply Rigidbody Constraints to game objects such as a character or a puzzle ball to prevent sideways tipping or unwanted vertical movement. Finally, you will design a small scene where a bouncy ball interacts with slippery ground and you’ll experiment by freezing specific rotation axes to compare rolling versus non-tumbling behavior. Each exercise is intended to reinforce test-driven tuning: change a value, run the scene, observe, and repeat. This repetition builds intuition so you can choose the right material settings and constraints for a desired gameplay feel without guesswork.

A Physics Material is an asset that defines how two surfaces interact when they collide. It packages three essential concepts: static friction, dynamic friction, and bounciness. Static friction resists the onset of motion, so a high static friction means an object sitting on a slope or surface needs more force to start moving. Dynamic friction applies once the object is already sliding, controlling how quickly it slows down. Bounciness, or restitution, controls how much collision energy is retained — zero means no bounce, one is a perfectly elastic collision. These properties are not applied in isolation; Unity also uses combine modes to resolve interactions between two materials. For example, a rubber ball hitting slippery ice will use a combination rule to determine the effective friction and bounce. A common misconception is thinking friction values correspond to real-world units; instead treat them as tuning parameters that shape feel in play mode. As a concrete example, creating a 'SuperBouncy' material with low friction and high bounce will make a sphere both slide and rebound, while a 'SlipperyIce' material with very low static and dynamic friction and low bounce will allow extended sliding with little rebound. The key takeaway is to think of Physics Materials as design tools for predictable interaction rather than exact physical replicas.

Creating a Physics Material in Unity is a simple workflow that yields immediate, testable results. Start in the Project window, right-click, choose Create → Physics Material, and give it a descriptive name like 'SlipperyIce' or 'SuperBouncy.' Open the material and set Dynamic Friction, Static Friction, and Bounciness to your desired values. Next choose Friction Combine and Bounce Combine modes that reflect how you want interactions to resolve when two materials meet. After configuration, select the GameObject with a Collider and drag the new Physics Material into the Collider's Material field in the Inspector. Run the scene and observe collisions to refine values. A useful habit is to create small test scenes with a plane and a sphere to iterate quickly. If you need the surface to always be slippery regardless of the other object, consider using Minimum for friction to favor the lower value. Remember to test both static and dynamic behavior: place an object on the surface to observe static friction, and nudge it or drop it to observe dynamic friction and bounciness. This process-focused approach keeps tuning efficient and repeatable.

Static and dynamic friction address two distinct phases of motion and both matter for believable interactions. Static friction is what keeps a resting object from sliding: it resists the initial force you apply. Dynamic friction comes into play after the object is moving; it slows the object while it slides or rolls. Consider a crate on a slope: if static friction is high, the crate will not start sliding until you apply a significant push. Once it starts sliding, the dynamic friction controls how quickly it slows down. This distinction matters for gameplay because you may want objects that resist small nudges but still slide freely once pushed, or surfaces that are equally reluctant to start and continue sliding. A common misconception is setting static lower than dynamic; typically static should be equal or higher than dynamic to simulate realistic stick-slip behavior. In practice, tune static for how hard it is to start movement, and dynamic for how objects behave while moving. Use concrete tests: place an object at rest to observe static friction, apply force to observe the threshold, then observe sliding to refine dynamic friction. This approach gives you control over both initiation and sustained motion.

Bounciness determines how much kinetic energy a collision keeps. Zero bounciness looks like clay: the object won't rebound. High bounciness resembles rubber or a super ball. Unity resolves a collision between two materials by applying the chosen Bounce Combine mode. Modes typically include Average, Minimum, Maximum, and Multiply. Average takes the mean of two bounciness values, Minimum picks the lower, Maximum picks the higher, and Multiply scales them together. The same concept applies to friction with Friction Combine modes. For example, if a rubber ball hits a sticky surface, using Maximum for bounce lets the higher bounciness dominate so the ball still appears lively. Using Minimum for friction means a slippery surface will remain slippery even against a high-friction object. A practical tip: Multiply often produces realistic friction because it scales down when either surface is low in friction; try it when you want surfaces to preserve 'weakness' like ice. A misconception is assuming bounce is independent of mass; while bounciness influences rebound, mass and collision context still affect final motion. Test bounciness with controlled drops and tune combine modes to achieve the intended gameplay effect.

Friction Combine modes determine the effective friction when two Physics Materials meet. Average calculates the mean of both friction values, which often produces moderate results. Minimum picks the lower of the two values, and is useful when you want a slippery surface to remain slippery despite contact with a rough object — for example, ice that stays slick even when a heavy boot collides with it. Maximum picks the higher value, which you might use when you want at least one object to contribute high friction, such as a highly grippy boot contacting any floor. Multiply multiplies the two values together and often produces realistic outcomes by scaling friction down when either surface is low. Consider numeric examples: 0.2 * 0.8 = 0.16 shows how Multiply yields lower combined friction when one surface is slippery. A common design choice is Multiply for friction and Maximum or Average for bounce depending on how you want bounciness to show. The practical workflow is to try each combine mode in a small test and choose the mode that matches your physical intuition and gameplay needs.

Physics Materials are applied to Collider components. Common colliders include Mesh Collider, Box Collider, Sphere Collider, and Plane. When you drag a Physics Material onto a Collider's Material field in the Inspector, that Collider inherits friction and bounciness settings for collisions. Remember that the collision outcome uses both colliders' materials and their combine modes, so both sides matter. In a scene where a ball rolls on a floor, you typically assign a material to both the ball's Sphere Collider and the ground's Mesh or Plane Collider to achieve the intended interaction. A useful architecture approach is to keep commonly used materials in a 'Materials' project folder with descriptive names like SuperBouncy and SlipperyIce, then reuse them across objects. If many objects share the same behavior, reusing a single Physics Material reduces maintenance and avoids inconsistent results. When debugging unexpected behavior, check collider assignments first, then Rigidbody mass and constraints; often surprising collisions come from an unassigned or incorrectly combined material rather than code errors.
